extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novelists), especially those learning scene/sequel structure (romance/paranormal writers included)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for fiction writers on recognizing, writing, and balancing Dwight Swain–style goal-focused Scenes and reaction-focused Sequels in narrative passages (including tricky cases like sex scenes and mixed-POV passages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene components (Goal - Conflict - Disaster)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes are made up of: Goal: What the protagonist wants at the beginning of the scene. Conflict: The obstacles standing in the way. Disaster: The outcome, what happens that prevents the protagonist from reaching their goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think: Scenes consist of Goals and Setbacks as characters take action to move the story forward. Scenes are goal-focused passages showing characters taking action to make progress toward a goal. A Disaster may be a failure to reach the goal or an event that forces reevaluation and sets up a Sequel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequel components (Reaction - Dilemma - Decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequels are made up of: Reaction: How the character reacts to the Disaster. Dilemma: The choice the character faces because of the Disaster. Decision: What the character decides to do next (new goal or new attempt to reach old goal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think: Sequels consist of Reacting and Analyzing as characters absorb and apply the lessons learned. Sequels are reaction-focused passages that process the Disaster and produce a new direction or decision for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to tell Scene vs Sequel (cause and effect test)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether a passage is a Scene or a Sequel, look at context: what is the cause and what is the effect? If the passage is about conscious actions and/or moving forward after a decision and yet leading to (causing) a reevaluation/realization, it's most likely a Scene. If it's about reacting to something that triggers a reevaluation and leads to a decision on how to move forward, it's most likely a Sequel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the passage's causal role in the chain: Scenes cause Sequel reactions; Sequels process Disasters and cause new Scene goals. Examine surrounding paragraphs to judge whether the passage is proactive (Scene) or reactive (Sequel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict definition broadened (internal and non-physical obstacles count)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict in a Scene is not limited to physical fights; it also includes internal conflict, reader/story tension, characters avoiding or suppressing conflict, and obstacles related to overall story goals rather than just the scene goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of sex-scene obstacles that function as Conflict: conversation probing each other's thoughts, misinterpretation, dramatic irony (readers know more about the other character), power struggles, worries about others' judgment, conflicting goals (romance vs career), emotional control, denial of feelings, fear of pursuing desires. If such internal issues lead to a Scene's Disaster, they are acting as Scene Conflict rather than Sequel material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disaster as Sequel trigger (Disaster may be reevaluation rather than simple failure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Scene's Disaster can be any outcome that pushes a character into reevaluation — not necessarily a clear failure to reach the immediate goal. That reevaluation is the trigger for the following Sequel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: teasing during sex isn't a Disaster for the sex act, but it can trigger a deeper appreciation (Sequel) in the POV character. Disasters can thus be subtle emotional moments that shift priorities and set up new decisions or goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length norms for Scenes and Sequels
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes are typically several paragraphs to pages or even a whole chapter. Sequels, in modern genre writing, are typically much shorter — from a sentence or two to paragraphs or a few pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are guidelines, not hard rules; the right length depends on genre, pacing needs, importance of the beat, and the story's goals. Use length to control pacing and reader breath between action beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequels' narrative functions (what good Sequels should accomplish)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequels should help readers relate to the character and know what to root for next; give insights into a character's internal goals and motivations; keep readers in the loop when a character pivots to a new goal; control pacing (slow down or give readers a breather from action); strengthen the story's stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing, ask whether a Sequel is accomplishing one or more of these functions; if not, the passage may need revision or removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-scene rubric: must contain Conflict/Disaster or be purposeful
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can't find any way a sex scene includes Conflict or a Disaster, the scene may be gratuitous — not adding to story, plot, or character change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Would anything change in the story, plot, or characters if the scene were cut? If not, consider cutting it or revising it so it affects character relationships, causes internal realizations, or sets new goals. Note that sex scenes can contain both Scene and Sequel moments and may shift POVs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-s scenes can contain many Scenes and Sequels (POV and layering)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single storytelling scene (small-s scene) can include multiple goal-focused Scenes and reaction-focused Sequels, often across different POV perspectives, which can make a passage feel like both Scene and Sequel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a sex scene may start as a Scene for one POV character, include a short Sequel moment, then pivot to a new Scene as the POV's goal changes. Analyze by breaking the passage into cause-effect micro-arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing Scenes and Sequels (no universal ratio; context-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single correct percentage or ratio of Scenes to Sequels. The right balance depends on story, genre, pacing needs, size of turning points, reader-emotion goals, and the author's intentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some genres emphasize action/Scenes; others emphasize emotion/Sequels. 'Twisty' plots may need more Sequels to explain shifting priorities. The balance should change across the story: some moments require longer Sequels, others only brief reactions. Understand your story and goals to choose the right balance rather than aiming for a fixed numeric target.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to judge whether Sequels are doing their job
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate Sequels by whether they produce clear character processing and decisions that set up the next Scene, clarify motivations, adjust stakes, or control pacing as intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a Sequel doesn't lead to a meaningful Decision or fails to reorient the character toward a new/renewed goal, it may be too weak or unnecessary. Use Sequels purposefully to create cause-and-effect chains that propel the story forward.
